newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Budget no boost to Australian government -polls.
newsitem.headline: Budget no boost to Australian government -polls.

text.p: The Australian government's cautious 1997/98 budget, which offered tax rebates and no real shocks, has failed to turn its popularity around, two opinion polls showed on Tuesday.

The Bulletin newsweekly's Morgan poll and The Australian newspaper's Newspoll put the Liberal-National government's lead over the Labor opposition at three to four points, well down on the 12-point gap just over a month ago.

Prime Minister John Howard had said he hoped the May 13 budget for the fiscal year from July would halt his administration's slide after its popularity fell to its lowest levels since its landslide election win 14 months ago.
The Morgan poll showed the government's support fell to 38.5 percent from 42 percent, while Labor's increased to 35.5 percent from 30 percent.
The Australian's poll showed the government's backing up one point to 41 percent and Labor's down two to 37 percent.
All of the main polls now show the gap around four points.
The coalition won power in March, 1996, with a vote of 47.3 percent against Labor's 38.8 percent.
But Howard retains a strong lead over Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley as preferred prime minister, said Newspoll.
The poll found Howard's rating steady at 45 percent and Beazley's up five points to 27 percent.
Both polls were conducted with nationwide samples of more than 1,000 voters over the past eight days.

The Morgan poll surveyed voters both before and after the May 13 budget and pollster Gary Morgan said the budget -- which cut the deficit and offered tax breaks for savers -- had not changed voters' opinions.
Instead, Morgan attributed the slide in government support on its handling of a lingering Aboriginal land rights dispute and an attack by Howard on populist politician Pauline Hanson.
Support for Hanson's fledgling One Nation party was unchanged at nine percent according to Newspoll and down one point to 12.5 percent in the Morgan poll.
